name: Oil price to Canadian dollar daily link (Ferraro, Rogoff, Rossi)

origin.source_title: Can oil prices forecast exchange rates? An empirical analysis of the relationship between commodity prices and exchange rates (Journal of International Money and Finance 54, 116-141, 2015; NBER WP 17998)

how_it_works.simple: Canada sells a lot of oil. On days when oil goes up, the Canadian dollar usually goes up too. The trick is whether yesterday's oil move tells you anything about today's currency move.
how_it_works.analogy: Like a shop whose takings rise on days the weather is good; knowing today's weather helps, knowing yesterday's helps much less.
how_it_works.precise: Regress daily changes in USD/CAD on daily oil price changes over a rolling window. Same-day oil changes give a strongly significant out-of-sample fit at daily frequency (but not monthly or quarterly). With lagged oil changes the predictive ability is ephemeral and shows up only in some subsamples (around 2006-2007) once instability is allowed for.

rule: Each day, estimate a rolling regression of daily CAD/USD returns on the prior day's oil return; if the fitted forecast for tomorrow is positive go long CAD vs USD, if negative go short, holding one day.
data_needed: Daily WTI or Brent oil price (e.g. FRED DCOILWTICO)
Optional: Canadian and US short-term interest rates
economic_rationale: Oil is Canada's main commodity export, so oil price shocks move Canada's terms of trade and the Canadian dollar (Ferraro, Rogoff and Rossi 2015).
why_it_might_fail: The authors find the lagged relationship is ephemeral and the link vanishes at monthly and quarterly frequencies, so a tradable edge is unlikely after costs. Kohlscheen et al. (2017) also find lagged commodity prices beat the random walk in only a few countries.

reported_results.notes: Forecast tests only, no trading returns. Same-day oil changes beat the random walk in daily out-of-sample fit; lagged oil changes beat it significantly only around 2006-2007 per the Fluctuation test.

post_publication_evidence: Kohlscheen, Avalos and Schrimpf (2017, IJCB) confirm the same-day link for CAD (RMSE ratio 0.850 vs random walk, 2009-2015) but find lagged commodity prices add little forecasting power, consistent with the original paper.

relevance.reason: Easy to test with free FRED data and directly about commodities driving FX, but the evidence says the tradable lagged effect is weak.
